steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Versions and implementations" section of an encyclopedia article on the AWK programming language: its original version and later revision, and a rundown of the main implementations that exist today.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Original AWK and Version 7 Unix
- 1985 expansion: "new awk" / nawk
- AWK-to-C and C++ translators
- BWK awk (the "One True AWK")
- gawk and its extensions
- Other implementations (mawk, awka, tawk, Jawk, xgawk, Hawk, BusyBox, etc.)
- Pointer to further lists

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Original AWK
  - written 1977
  - distributed with Version 7 Unix
- New awk
  - 1985: authors start expanding the language; biggest addition user-defined functions
  - described in book The AWK Programming Language (1988)
  - implementation shipped in UNIX System V releases
  - called "new awk" / nawk to avoid confusion with incompatible old version
  - released under free software license 1996; still maintained by Brian Kernighan
- Translators
  - old Unix (e.g. UNIX/32V) had awkcc: AWK -> C
  - Kernighan wrote awk -> C++ program; state unknown
- BWK awk
  - aka nawk; Kernighan's version
  - "One True AWK": term used with the book; Kernighan an original author
  - FreeBSD: one-true-awk
  - features not in book: tolower, ENVIRON; FIXES file in source archive
  - used by Android, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, macOS, illumos
  - main contributors to repo: Brian Kernighan, Arnold Robbins
- gawk (GNU awk)
  - free software; only implementation making serious progress on i18n/l10n and TCP/IP networking
  - written before original became freely available
  - own debugger; profiler for measured performance enhancements
  - extend with shared libraries
  - default AWK in some Linux distributions
  - version 5.2 (September 2022): persistent memory - remembers script-defined variables/functions between invocations, passes data between unrelated scripts (Persistent-Memory gawk User Manual)
  - gawk-csv: CSV extension, CSV input/output
- Other implementations
  - mawk: very fast, Mike Brennan, bytecode interpreter
  - libmawk: fork of mawk, embed multiple parallel awk interpreters
  - awka: front end on mawk; translates AWK -> C; statically linked with libawka.a; much faster, compares well with other AWKs, Perl, Tcl (author's tests); small scripts -> 160–170 kB programs
  - tawk (Thompson AWK): compiler for Solaris, MS-DOS, OS/2, Windows; sold by Thompson Automation Software (defunct)
  - Jawk: Java; originally SourceForge, now maintained elsewhere; embeddable in Java apps; Java extensions add functions
  - xgawk: gawk fork, dynamically loadable libraries; XMLgawk extension merged into GNU Awk 4.1.0
  - Hawk: embeddable AWK interpreter in C, on Github; began as QSEAWK in QSE library
  - libfawk: very small, function-only, reentrant, embeddable, C
  - BusyBox AWK: Dmitry Zakharov; very small, for embedded systems
  - CLAWK: Michael Parker; Common Lisp; built on his regex library
  - goawk: Go, Ben Hoyt, some convenience extensions, Github
- gawk manual lists more implementations

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
AWK was first written in 1977, and it was distributed with Version 7 Unix.

In 1985 the authors started to expand the language. The most important addition was user-defined functions. This language is described in the book The AWK Programming Language, which was published in 1988, and the implementation was made available in UNIX System V releases. Because it was incompatible with the older version, this version was sometimes called "new awk" or nawk so people would not confuse them. In 1996 this implementation was released under a free software license and Brian Kernighan still maintains it.

Old Unix versions such as UNIX/32V included a program called awkcc, which converted AWK to C. Kernighan also wrote a program that turns awk into C++, but its state is not known.

BWK awk, which is also known as nawk, is the version by Brian Kernighan. People call it the "One True AWK" because the term was used in connection with the book that first described the language, and because Kernighan was one of the original authors of AWK. FreeBSD calls this version one-true-awk. This version also has some features that are not in the book, for example tolower and ENVIRON, and the FIXES file in the source archive has the details. Android, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, macOS, and illumos all use this version. The main contributors to the nawk source repository are Brian Kernighan and Arnold Robbins.

gawk (GNU awk) is another free-software implementation. It is the only implementation that makes serious progress on internationalization and localization and on TCP/IP networking. It was written before the original implementation was freely available. It has its own debugger, and it has a profiler so the user can make measured performance enhancements to a script. Users can also extend it with shared libraries. Some Linux distributions use gawk as their default AWK. Since version 5.2 (September 2022) gawk has a persistent memory feature, which can remember variables and functions defined in a script from one invocation to the next, and can pass data between scripts that are not related, as the Persistent-Memory gawk User Manual describes.

- gawk-csv: CSV extension of gawk, CSV input/output
- mawk: very fast, Mike Brennan, bytecode interpreter
- libmawk: fork of mawk, embed multiple parallel awk interpreters
- awka: front end on mawk; AWK -> C; statically linked with libawka.a; much faster, compares well with other AWKs, Perl, Tcl (author's tests); small scripts -> 160–170 kB programs
- tawk (Thompson AWK): compiler for Solaris, MS-DOS, OS/2, Windows; sold by Thompson Automation Software (defunct)
- Jawk: Java; originally SourceForge, now maintained elsewhere; embeddable; Java extensions
- xgawk: gawk fork, dynamically loadable libraries; XMLgawk merged into GNU Awk 4.1.0
- Hawk: embeddable, C, Github; began as QSEAWK in QSE library
- libfawk: very small, function-only, reentrant, embeddable, C
- BusyBox AWK: Dmitry Zakharov; very small, embedded systems
- CLAWK: Michael Parker; Common Lisp; his regex library
- goawk: Go, Ben Hoyt, convenience extensions, Github
- gawk manual lists more implementations

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
AWK was first written in 1977, and it was distributed with Version 7 Unix.

In 1985 the authors started to expand the language. The most important addition was user-defined functions. This language is described in the book The AWK Programming Language, which was published in 1988, and the implementation was made available in UNIX System V releases. Because it was incompatible with the older version, this version was sometimes called "new awk" or nawk so people would not confuse them. In 1996 this implementation was released under a free software license and Brian Kernighan still maintains it.

Old Unix versions such as UNIX/32V included a program called awkcc, which converted AWK to C. Kernighan also wrote a program that turns awk into C++, but its state is not known.

BWK awk, which is also known as nawk, is the version by Brian Kernighan. People call it the "One True AWK" because the term was used in connection with the book that first described the language, and because Kernighan was one of the original authors of AWK. FreeBSD calls this version one-true-awk. This version also has some features that are not in the book, for example tolower and ENVIRON, and the FIXES file in the source archive has the details. Android, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, macOS, and illumos all use this version. The main contributors to the nawk source repository are Brian Kernighan and Arnold Robbins.

gawk (GNU awk) is another free-software implementation. It is the only implementation that makes serious progress on internationalization and localization and on TCP/IP networking. It was written before the original implementation was freely available. It has its own debugger, and it has a profiler so the user can make measured performance enhancements to a script. Users can also extend it with shared libraries. Some Linux distributions use gawk as their default AWK. Since version 5.2 (September 2022) gawk has a persistent memory feature, which can remember variables and functions defined in a script from one invocation to the next, and can pass data between scripts that are not related, as the Persistent-Memory gawk User Manual describes.

gawk-csv is the CSV extension of gawk, and it lets you input and output data in CSV format.

mawk is an AWK implementation by Mike Brennan. It is very fast and it is based on a bytecode interpreter.

libmawk is a fork of mawk. It lets applications embed multiple awk interpreters that run in parallel.

awka is another program that translates AWK scripts into C code, and its front end is written on top of the mawk program. When the result is compiled and the author's libawka.a is statically included, the executables are much faster, and the author's tests say they compare very well with other versions of AWK, Perl, or Tcl. Small scripts become programs of 160–170 kB.

tawk (Thompson AWK) is an AWK compiler for Solaris, MS-DOS, OS/2, and Windows. It was sold by Thompson Automation Software, which is defunct.

Jawk is an implementation of AWK written in Java. It was developed on SourceForge at first and it is now maintained somewhere else. You can embed it in Java applications, and it supports extensions written in Java which add functions to AWK scripts.

xgawk is a fork of gawk which extends gawk with libraries that can be dynamically loaded. Its XMLgawk extension was integrated into the official GNU Awk release 4.1.0.

Hawk is an AWK interpreter written in C that can be embedded, and it is hosted on Github. It started as QSEAWK, which was an embedded AWK interpreter in the QSE library.

libfawk is an interpreter written in C which is very small, function-only, reentrant and embeddable.

BusyBox has an AWK implementation by Dmitry Zakharov. It is very small and suitable for embedded systems.

CLAWK, by Michael Parker, is an AWK implementation in Common Lisp. It is based on the regular expression library by the same author.

goawk is an AWK implementation in Go by Ben Hoyt with a few convenience extensions. It is hosted on Github.

There is a list of more AWK implementations in the gawk manual.

steps.text:
AWK was originally written in 1977 and distributed with Version 7 Unix.

In 1985 its authors started expanding the language, most significantly by adding user-defined functions. The language is described in the book The AWK Programming Language, published 1988, and its implementation was made available in releases of UNIX System V. This implementation was released under a free software license in 1996 and is still maintained by Brian Kernighan.

Old versions of Unix, such as UNIX/32V, included awkcc, which converted AWK to C. Kernighan also wrote a program to turn awk into C++; its current state is not known.[1]

BWK awk, also known as nawk, is the version by Brian Kernighan. CLAWK by Michael Parker is an AWK implementation in Common Lisp, based on the author's own regular expression library.[10]
